deed: Ernst Boris Chain developed penicillin into a drug and won the Nobel Prize in Medicine
title: Ernst Chain, a Jewish refugee from Berlin, turned penicillin into a medicine and won the Nobel Prize

trailer.text: Ernst Boris Chain, a Jew born in Berlin, shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Fleming and Florey.
As late as the 1940s, minor cuts and scrapes could still be fatal.
At the beginning of the 1940s, Chain, Florey and their colleagues succeeded in systematically producing pure penicillin and studying its properties.
By 1943, the drug went into regular medical use for Allied troops.

glance.value: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 1945

paragraphs.text: Ernst Boris Chain was born on June 19, 1906, in Berlin.
He was the son of Dr. Michael Chain, a chemist and industrialist.
His father died when Ernst was only 13.
Chain was of Russian-German-Jewish descent.
When Hitler came to power, Chain understood that his days in Germany were numbered.
He was forced to flee Germany.
According to JTA, he had been a British citizen since 1939 and was a lecturer at Oxford University.
His mother and sister stayed in Berlin, and eventually perished in a concentration camp.
As late as the 1940s, minor cuts and scrapes could still be fatal.
When a bacterial infection spread into the bloodstream, there was very little physicians could do.
In 1924 Calvin Coolidge Jr, the son of the US President, died of an infection, a week after a tennis game.
Penicillin proved to be an unstable substance, difficult to produce in pure form.
Fleming did not think penicillin could be mass-produced, and he stopped working on it in the 1930s.
He became convinced that it would be impossible to turn the mould solution into a useable drug, and turned to other projects.
Chain and Florey decided to study antibacterial substances produced by micro-organisms, among them penicillin.
According to Encyclopedia.com, Chain emphasized that only purely scientific curiosity had motivated him to begin studying penicillin.
In early 1940 the Rockefeller Foundation granted the Dunn School a research grant of £1,500 for a period of 12 months.
At the beginning of their penicillin work, Chain and Florey were frustrated by a lack of support from the Medical Research Council.
Chain and Edward Abraham developed a successful technique for purifying and concentrating penicillin.
According to Cambridge, it was Heatley who devised the back-extraction technique for purifying penicillin in bulk.
In the early process, many gallons of mold broth were needed to produce a small amount, one that covered a fingernail.

stations.title: From the mice to the policeman

paragraphs.text: In March 1940 Chain asked that two mice be injected with a sample of penicillin that he and Abraham had extracted.

On 25 May eight mice were infected with haemolytic streptococci, and four of them received penicillin; 16.5 hours later the four mice that had received penicillin were alive, and the mice that had not been treated had died.
On August 24, 1940, Florey and Chain reported their findings in the Lancet.
In February 1941 a policeman became the first patient with an infection to be treated with penicillin in the hope of a cure.
His condition initially improved.
But the penicillin ran out before he fully recovered, and his condition worsened.

stations.title: From bedpans to a factory in Peoria

paragraphs.text: Many vessels were used to grow the mould, including hospital bedpans and hundreds of specially ordered ceramic pots.
Heatley asked a Staffordshire pottery to produce 500 ceramic pots.
At the beginning of July 1941, Florey and Heatley flew across the Atlantic to win US assistance.
According to the Linda Hall Library, the team co-opted a factory of incubating tanks in Peoria, Illinois, and soon mass quantities of penicillin were available.
By 1943, the drug went into regular medical use for Allied troops.
In the autumn of 1943, military doctors could obtain penicillin in large quantities to treat the battle wounded.
By 1944, the United States produced forty times more penicillin than Britain.
Chain and Abraham proposed that a four-membered beta-lactam ring lay at the heart of the penicillin molecule.
According to Encyclopedia.com, the structure proposed by Chain and his partners turned out to be correct.
Later it turned out that the accumulation of 6-aminopenicillanic acid in the fermentation liquid was decisive.
It made it possible to produce new penicillins of a desired structure on an industrial scale.

According to an encyclopedia, Chain was a consultant to the British pharmaceutical company Beecham, but his involvement in the later work, after the company's scientists had stayed at his centre in Rome, is not clear.
According to Encyclopedia.com, Chain and his partners proposed the correct structure by October 1943
Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Fleming and Florey.
The prize was awarded "for the discovery of penicillin and its curative effect in various infectious diseases".
According to the Royal College of Physicians (RCP), Chain's contribution was vital, and his enthusiasm and devotion were decisive for the success of the work.
In 1954 Chain received the Paul Ehrlich Centenary Prize.
He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society.
In 1969 Queen Elizabeth II knighted him.
The biochemistry building at Imperial College London is named after him.
Chain died on August 12, 1979.
According to NobelPrize.org, in 1949

stations.title: Arguments, a patent and those left out

paragraphs.text: Chain urged that a patent be sought on penicillin, but Florey refused.
This decision angered Chain for years.
Chain had a volatile temperament that was bound to clash with Florey's quick temper.
According to the RCP, there was much argument about the relative contributions of Fleming, Chain and Florey.
Over time, the simple story of an absent-minded scientist who made a discovery by accident proved more appealing than the story of the complex technical development.
Because of the rule limiting the prize to three winners, Heatley was left out of the prize, as was the rest of the team at Oxford and in Peoria.
The Nobel Prize Committee did not mention the Penicillin Girls, although their work was crucial to scaling up production in Oxford.

disagreements.question: In what year did the systematic research begin?

versions.says: According to the Science History Institute, Florey and Chain decided in 1938 to study antibacterial substances, among them penicillin
According to NobelPrize.org, Chain and Florey began the systematic research in 1939

disagreements.question: How many patients were treated in the first trials, and what happened to them?

versions.says: According to Oxfordshire Blue Plaques, six patients were selected for the first trial and four made a complete recovery; the policeman Albert Alexander, the first patient, relapsed when there was not enough purified penicillin, and died on 15 March 1941

According to the Oxford case study, in the full clinical trials conducted later under the supervision of Ethel Florey, penicillin was given to 15 seriously ill patients and to 172 patients with localised infections.
According to the Science History Institute, Chain and Edward Abraham developed a successful technique for purifying and concentrating
According to Cambridge, it was Heatley who devised the back-extraction technique for purifying in bulk

disagreements.question: When did Chain return to England and become a professor at Imperial College?

versions.says: According to NobelPrize.org, he became Professor of Biochemistry at Imperial College in 1961
According to Encyclopedia.com, he was persuaded to return to England in 1963
According to the RCP, he returned to London in 1964 to take charge of the new facilities
According to Encyclopedia.com, in Mulranny, Ireland, on August 12, 1979
According to the Linda Hall Library, in Castlebar, Ireland, in 1979

unknowns.text: The Penicillin Girls were Ruth Callow, Betty Cooke, Peggy Gardner, Claire Inayat, Patricia McKegney and Megan Lankester; the Nobel Prize Committee did not mention them, but their work was crucial to scaling up the production of penicillin in Oxford.
